prize_parts.citation: for the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of single DNA bases without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: After the full first round I keep base editing as a single-part prize for David Liu. It is the one shortlisted idea that I can state as a chemical transformation in a sentence: an engineered deaminase, tethered to a programmable scaffold, converts one base into another without a double-strand break. The adenine editor is the decisive piece, because no natural enzyme deaminates adenine in DNA and it had to be evolved, which is real enzymology and nucleobase chemistry. Four members include B061 and all four name Liu alone, so the attribution question is the least contested of any leading position in the chair's summary. It is a game-changer in my sense: completely new, reproduced by many laboratories, and already used in patients. It is also distinct from the 2020 prize, which recognised a programmable nuclease; here the chemical step is the point.
statement.case_against: I still see three real weaknesses. Clinical durability and off-target and bystander editing are unproven, so a critic can call the timing early. Nishida and Kondo's cytidine deaminase fusion appeared concurrently, and Komor and Gaudelli did the lead experiments. And two genome-editing prizes within about six years is a legitimate objection. I weigh the Nishida and Kondo point as follows: their work covers the cytosine deaminase concept only, whereas the adenine editor and the evolved deaminase, which carry the deepest chemistry, are Liu's alone, so I do not think it forces a second name, but I accept that it is the main priority risk and that the committee's expert report should settle it. I would not add Komor or Gaudelli, since a three-person cap is better spent on a clean attribution.

responses.point: Brzezinski proposes a two-part prize, Crews and Deshaies for degraders and Liu for base editing, presented as one achievement acting on proteins and one on nucleic acids.
responses.response: I have thought about this carefully, because it is the only configuration that combines the two most supported ballots and I agree with you that Crews and Deshaies hold the clearest priority for the heterobifunctional concept, and that Liu should stand alone. Where I stay put is the second part. The deciding test for me is evidence of consequences, and no approved degrader exists yet, so adding B007 would put a still-maturing field next to a field that is itself only about a decade old; I would be stacking two timing risks in one year. The pairing also rests on a loose symmetry, proteins versus nucleic acids, and not on a shared chemical principle. I would not oppose B007 as a part if the committee wants it, with Crews and Deshaies as the core, but I do not move my own preference to it.

responses.point: Chabes holds that Crews, Deshaies and Handa should be credited together, with Handa's identification of cereblon explaining thalidomide-type drugs as molecular glues and tying the PROTAC and glue strands into one principle, and says clinical maturity of base editing and degraders is similar.
responses.response: Your point that lenalidomide-type glue drugs already act in patients is fair, and it is a stronger maturity argument than the absence of an approved PROTAC suggests. I accept that cereblon is a discrete and decisive discovery. My difficulty is the citation: Handa's result is a mechanistic explanation of an existing drug, while Crews and Deshaies designed a new chemical operation, so I do not think one sentence covers both honestly, as Aili also argues. Attribution on B007 is therefore still the least settled on the list, with Ciulli, Handa, Sakamoto and others all credible for the third seat. I also do not agree that maturity cannot discriminate: base editing has the clearer single driver and earlier patient data, which makes its remaining risk smaller than the credit risk in B007. Your offer to support a two-part prize is noted but does not change my view.

responses.point: Linke pairs sequencing-by-synthesis (Balasubramanian and Klenerman, Rothberg excluded) with Liu, framed as reading and rewriting DNA, and asks whether I would accept dropping Rothberg for the sake of the pairing.
responses.response: Thank you for the direct question. I would accept Balasubramanian and Klenerman if the committee decided that sequencing belongs in this prize, because the reversible-terminator chemistry is theirs and it is the chemically decisive step. I still think the Rothberg exclusion is hard to defend publicly, since 454 was the first commercial massively parallel platform, and a prize built on dropping him invites exactly the attribution criticism you list. I also think much of the transformative power is instrumentation and engineering, and the 1980 prize already covers DNA sequencing, so the chemistry-versus-technology objection stays. Your pairing is the one closest to my own preference and I will keep B001 as an alternative, but a combined 'reading and rewriting' theme looks to me more like a bridge between first choices than a shared principle, so I keep Liu as a single part.

responses.point: Somfai pairs C-N coupling for Buchwald and Hartwig with Liu, and argues that Pd-amido chemistry needed new ligands and is a new capability, not a refinement of the 2010 prize.
responses.response: Your reply on C-N coupling changed my view somewhat: the Pd-amido problems of beta-hydride elimination and reductive elimination are real and they were solved by new ligand design, so I now regard B022 as a distinct departure and not just a continuation. I am glad you moved base editing into your configuration with Liu alone. I still do not put B022 in my own configuration, because it was ranked by only three members and Kosugi's earlier tin-amide coupling leaves a priority question. The 2010 overlap is a real cost for a prize whose headline is that it must be completely new, even if I now weigh it less.

uncertainties: Whether Nishida and Kondo's concurrent cytidine deaminase work is close enough to require crediting, which would turn a Liu-alone prize into a two- or three-person set.
Whether long-term safety and durability of base editing in patients are far enough along, and whether the committee treats the 2020 prize as making this a second genome-editing prize.
Whether the committee will accept a two-part prize built from first choices, and whether degraders (Crews and Deshaies, with a settled third name) are mature enough without an approved drug.
Whether sequencing is judged as chemistry and how Solexa and 454 credit could be divided within three seats.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate. My connections are Arieh Warshel (EVB collaboration) and the Uppsala ribosome and RNA community, which do not overlap with base editing, degraders, sequencing or the other shortlisted areas. I am a computational biochemist, so I judge base editing, degraders and sequencing as an informed outsider.
